question: Currently, each Member State can decide what is considered hazardous or non-hazardous waste, unless it falls within the list laid down in Directive 2008/98/EC. This complicates the administrative procedure when waste crosses the border to another Member State. In addition, if waste is considered hazardous, there is even more red tape.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1157, which will enter into application in May 2026 and will regulate the transport of waste destined for recovery, is meant to reduce the administrative burden. However, the text as it stands establishes requirements such as a notification procedure and the conclusion of a contract, which are much more cumbersome than the requirements for non-hazardous waste destined for recovery.
That additional burden prevents the smooth movement of hazardous waste to recovery centres. 1.

Does the Commission intend to review the possibility for Member States to establish additional categories of hazardous waste, given that this complicates the administrative procedures for waste crossing borders?

Does it plan to specifically monitor whether the implementation of Regulation (EU) 2024/1157 on shipments of waste will actually simplify and speed up the intra-EU movement of hazardous waste destined for recovery?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.1.2026) The EU has implemented procedural requirements regarding transboundary waste shipments in the EU in the form of Regulations since 19931. The rules have always been stricter for the shipment of hazardous waste, requiring a prior consent, pursuant to the Basel Convention2.

The classification of waste as hazardous or not is largely harmonised at EU level through the implementation of the Waste Framework Directive3 and the establishment of the European List of Waste4. This list is a comprehensive list of waste codes and descriptions used for classifying all wastes, distinguishing hazardous from non-hazardous waste.

The Waste Shipment Regulation5 empowers the Commission to identify, via delegated acts, specific non-hazardous waste streams which should be subject to the ‘green-list’ procedure for the purpose of shipments for recovery between Member States. The aim of this empowerment is to further harmonise the classification of waste for the purpose of shipping it between Member States, where needed.
A recent public consultation6 gathered information from stakeholders to prepare a delegated act ‘green-listing’ certain waste to facilitate the shipments of waste for recovery within the EU.

The Commission will, in the context of the review mandated by Article 84 of the Regulation, assess the efficiency of the procedure of prior written notification and consent by analysing elements such as the number of objections and consents, and the time between the submission of and a decision taken on a notification. The Commission may use data stored in the upcoming Digital Waste Shipment System7 for this purpose.
1 Council Regulation (EEC) No 259/93 of 1 February 1993 on the supervision and control of shipments of waste
